Family Health

Vaginal cysts: symptoms, assessment and treatment

Updated: October 11, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

A new lump inside the vagina or near its opening can be worrying. Many cysts are benign and cause little trouble, but you cannot identify every lump by touch or appearance. The useful first step is a clinician's examination, especially if a lump is changing, painful or new after menopause. Treatment depends on its exact location and cause rather than a single rule for all vaginal cysts.

A cyst is not the same as every vaginal lump

A vaginal cyst is a closed sac within or beneath the vaginal lining, often containing fluid or other material. The vagina is the internal canal; the vulva is the external genital area. A cyst on the vaginal wall differs anatomically from a Bartholin gland cyst near the vaginal entrance, although both may be described casually as a vaginal lump. Neither is an ovarian cyst.

Other conditions, including a prolapse, a urethral diverticulum, a benign solid growth or, less commonly, cancer can resemble a cyst. An itchy, sore or swollen area is not enough to diagnose one. Most diagnosed vaginal cysts are benign, but that is a reason for proportionate assessment, not a reason to ignore an unexplained lump.

Inclusion cysts and Gartner duct cysts

Inclusion cysts can form when tissue becomes trapped after a vaginal injury, repair of a childbirth tear or surgery. A previous procedure is useful history to tell the clinician, but not every person with a cyst has had an injury and a scar alone does not establish the diagnosis.

Gartner duct cysts develop from remnants of a duct present during fetal development, usually along a side wall of the vagina. They are not simply a leftover organ in the cervix. Other developmental cysts can occur too. Location and examination help distinguish these from a nearby urinary-tract problem; the name cannot reliably be decided at home.

Bartholin cysts and abscesses are a related but separate problem

The Bartholin glands lie near either side of the vaginal opening. If a duct becomes blocked, gland fluid can collect and form a usually one-sided cyst. A small cyst may be painless. If infection produces an abscess, pain, tenderness, heat, swelling, pus or fever can develop. A blocked duct does not necessarily mean an STI or poor hygiene.

A lump that becomes larger and more painful over hours or days, feels hot and tender, produces pus or is accompanied by fever or feeling unwell needs urgent same-day assessment. Do not wait several days to see whether a bath works. Seek immediate emergency help if you cannot pass urine, have confusion, breathing difficulty, fainting or severe rapidly worsening illness. For emergency care, do not drive yourself; ask someone to drive you or call an ambulance.

Symptoms and finding a cyst without symptoms

Many vaginal-wall cysts cause no symptoms and are found during an examination done for another reason. Others cause a noticeable lump, pressure, discomfort with penetration or tampon insertion, or urinary symptoms. Growth or infection may increase pain; itching is nonspecific and may have a different cause.

Arrange a clinical appointment for any new lump in or around the vagina, even if it is painless. Mention bleeding, unusual discharge, urinary changes, previous childbirth injury or surgery, and whether it has grown. You do not need repeated internal self-examinations or to insert a tampon to test it. Stop an activity that hurts, including sex, while arranging advice.

What examination, tests or biopsy may involve

A clinician asks about symptoms and history, then examines the vulva and, if appropriate, the vagina with your consent. You may ask for a chaperone and to pause or stop. Appearance and location often provide the main information. Swabs for infection or STI testing are selected for the symptoms and sexual history; routine tests for every asymptomatic cyst are not required.

Ultrasound may help when the diagnosis or anatomy is unclear or when planning surgery; MRI can be considered if more detail is needed. CT is not an automatic next step. A suspicious, solid, fixed, persistent or changing lesion may need biopsy. A new Bartholin-region lump at age 40 or older, or after menopause, deserves particular assessment and discussion of biopsy to exclude a rare cancer; this does not mean the lump is cancer or that every vaginal cyst needs biopsy.

Observation, drainage or removal

A small, stable, asymptomatic vaginal cyst can often be observed after diagnosis, with follow-up examinations agreed with the clinician. Increasing size, pain, difficult intercourse or tampon use, urinary symptoms, infection or concern about the diagnosis may change the plan. A symptomatic vaginal-wall cyst may be opened surgically to maintain drainage or removed; choices depend on its type, location and nearby structures.

An abscess may need professional drainage, with antibiotics when indicated; antibiotics alone are not a reliable answer for every abscess. For a Bartholin cyst or abscess, a Word catheter can maintain a drainage opening, or marsupialisation can stitch an opening in place. These procedures differ from simply puncturing a lump. Gland removal is usually reserved for selected recurrent or suspicious cases. Discuss alternatives, anaesthesia, benefits and risks rather than assuming all cysts require the same operation.

Comfort measures are not home drainage

For a diagnosed uncomplicated Bartholin cyst, a comfortably warm shallow bath may ease mild discomfort. This is a comfort measure, not a cure for every vaginal-wall cyst and not a reason to delay assessment of an abscess. Ask which pain relief is suitable, particularly during pregnancy or breastfeeding or if you have other conditions or medicines.

Do not squeeze, puncture, cut or try to drain a lump, or insert foods, essential oils or unprescribed products. Gentle external washing and drying may support comfort; internal douching does not prevent cysts. If a cyst opens by itself, keep the area clean and seek advice for persistent pain, fever, worsening swelling or discharge. Condoms reduce the risk of some STIs but cannot prevent every cyst, developmental remnant or childbirth-related inclusion cyst.

Recovery, complications and recurrence

Many cysts remain small and harmless, while some enlarge, become infected or press on nearby structures. Procedures can cause bleeding, infection, pain or scarring, and a cyst or abscess can recur. Removal is not a guarantee that it will never return. The chance of recurrence and the appropriate follow-up depend on the diagnosis and procedure.

Follow your own wound, catheter and activity instructions after treatment, including when to resume penetration, tampons, swimming and exercise. Do not manipulate or remove a catheter yourself. Contact the team for increasing pain, swelling, redness, pus, bad-smelling discharge, fever or wound opening. Heavy bleeding, inability to urinate or severe systemic illness needs immediate assessment; use emergency services for fainting, confusion or breathing difficulty. Ask how and when you will receive biopsy or culture results and who to contact if symptoms return. For emergency care, do not drive yourself; ask someone to drive you or call an ambulance.

A practical plan for your appointment

Record when you first noticed the lump, its symptoms, any change, urinary problems and relevant pregnancy, birth or surgery history. Ask what diagnosis is most likely, whether a test would change care, what observation means, and which symptoms should bring you back sooner. You can discuss discomfort and sexual concerns without being expected to continue painful penetration.

BeMama can help organise symptom notes and questions for the appointment. It cannot identify the lump, distinguish a cyst from a tumour or urinary problem, decide whether biopsy or drainage is needed, or exclude an urgent infection. A record or image in an app should not delay an examination or emergency help.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Arrange a clinician’s examination for any new lump in or around the vagina. Record when it appeared, symptoms, changes, urinary problems and relevant birth or surgery history. Ask for each examination step to be explained; you may request a chaperone, a pause or a stop.

Ask what diagnosis is most likely and whether observation, imaging, biopsy or a procedure would change your care. Discuss benefits, risks, possible recurrence and when to return; do not assume every cyst needs the same operation or every test.

Follow your individual wound, catheter and activity instructions and ask how to receive results and who to contact if symptoms return. Do not squeeze, puncture or drain a lump or remove a catheter yourself, and do not delay assessment of warning signs with home remedies.

How BeMama can help

BeMama can help you record symptoms, changes and questions for a clinical appointment. It cannot diagnose a vaginal lump, rule out cancer or a urinary problem, assess an abscess, choose biopsy or drainage, or exclude an emergency. Seek examination or urgent care for warning signs regardless of the app.

When to seek help

Arrange assessment of any new vaginal or vulvar lump, especially a new Bartholin-region lump from age 40 or after menopause. Rapid growth, increasing pain, heat, redness, pus, fever or feeling unwell needs urgent same-day care. Inability to pass urine needs immediate emergency care. Heavy bleeding or severe rapidly worsening illness needs immediate assessment; fainting, confusion or breathing difficulty needs emergency services now. Do not squeeze, puncture, drain or delay with home remedies. For emergency care, do not drive yourself; ask someone to drive you or call an ambulance.

Evidence notes updated: October 11, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Vaginal-wall cysts, Bartholin cysts and ovarian cysts are different; a new lump needs examination rather than self-diagnosis.
  • Small diagnosed symptom-free cysts may be observed. Tests, biopsy and procedures are chosen for symptoms, location and concerning findings.
  • Rapid growth with increasing pain, pus, fever or feeling unwell needs same-day help. Inability to urinate or severe systemic illness needs immediate care.
  • Do not squeeze or drain a lump yourself. Follow individual aftercare and results plans, because recurrence is possible even after treatment.

Frequently asked questions

What symptoms can a vaginal cyst cause?

Many have no symptoms. A lump, pressure, pain with penetration or tampon insertion, or urinary symptoms may occur. Itching or swelling alone does not prove a cyst. Have any new lump examined; rapidly increasing pain, pus, fever or illness needs urgent same-day care.

What complications can occur?

A cyst may grow, become painful, get infected or press on nearby structures. Treatment can cause bleeding, infection or scarring, and recurrence is possible. Seek prompt advice for worsening symptoms and immediate emergency help for inability to urinate, confusion, breathing difficulty or fainting. For emergency care, do not drive yourself; ask someone to drive you or call an ambulance.

How are vaginal cysts treated?

After diagnosis, a stable symptom-free cyst may need observation only. Symptomatic or concerning cysts may need surgery; an abscess may require drainage with antibiotics when indicated. Bartholin treatments include a Word catheter or marsupialisation in selected cases. No single treatment or permanent-cure guarantee applies to all cysts.

How can a cyst be found if there are no obvious symptoms?

A clinician may notice it during an examination for another reason. Some cysts relate to previous birth injury or surgery, others to developmental remnants or blocked ducts. Do not repeatedly probe yourself to search for one. A warm bath can ease mild discomfort from a diagnosed uncomplicated Bartholin cyst, but does not diagnose or cure all vaginal cysts.

Does every lump need imaging or biopsy?

No. Examination often guides the diagnosis. Ultrasound, MRI, infection tests or biopsy are used when findings or symptoms justify them. A new Bartholin-area lump from age 40 or after menopause should be assessed carefully, with biopsy considered to exclude a rare cancer; age alone does not diagnose cancer.

Can I prevent cysts or drain one at home?

There is no guaranteed prevention for every type. Condoms reduce some STI risks but do not prevent all blocked ducts, developmental cysts or inclusion cysts. Never squeeze, puncture or drain a lump yourself, and do not douche or insert remedies. Seek advice rather than waiting on a home treatment when pain or swelling worsens.

What should I ask after a procedure?

Ask about wound and catheter care, suitable pain relief, activity and sex restrictions, warning signs, results and follow-up. Do not remove a catheter yourself. Increasing pain, pus, bad smell or fever needs urgent advice; heavy bleeding, inability to pass urine or severe illness needs immediate care.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
